data.name: Ottilia
data.long_meaning: Derived from the Latin word 'otulus' meaning 'wealth'. The name Ottilia is a feminine form, and it means 'wealth in God'. In Christianity, it is the name of several saints, including Saint Ottilia of Bavaria, who was a wealthy noblewoman who renounced her riches and dedicated her life to God.

data.cultural_impact: The name Ottilia has its origins in the Latin language and means 'wealth'. Historically, wealth was a symbol of power, prestige, and security. However, in the context of this name, wealth is connected to God. Naming a child Ottilia signifies a hope that they will be blessed with spiritual wealth and happiness, rather than just material wealth.
data.spiritual_significance: The spiritual significance of the name Ottilia lies in its connection to God. For Christians, the name Ottilia represents the desire and hope to be wealthy in the eyes of God. It is a reminder of the importance of seeking spiritual riches over material possessions. It also celebrates the journey of Saint Ottilia, a noblewoman who renounced her wealth and dedicated her life to God, making her an inspiration for those who seek to live a life centered around faith and spiritual growth.

historical_references.reference: Ottilia, the granddaughter of St. Boniface, was the founder and first abbess of the double monastery at Heidenheim in Swabia, Germany. She is venerated as a patron saint of the diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart. The monastery was established around 775 AD.
historical_references.context: Double monastery was a monastic institution in the Early Middle Ages where men and women lived as a community under the same rule and obeyed the same abbot or abbess. Ottilia was the founder and the first abbess of such a monastery at Heidenheim in Swabia, Germany.

historical_references.reference: Ottilia of Maasland (also known as Ottilie of Egmond) was a Dutch saint who lived in the 11th century. She was the daughter of Count Dirk III of Holland and was married to Count Gerard I of the House of Egmont. She became a hermit after her husband's death around 1037 AD and died around 1044 AD. She is venerated as a patron saint of the Netherlands.
